scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance traces back to traditional African-American plantation dances like the Juba and challenge step routines.
James P. Johnson recalled hearing its signature beat from dockworkers in Charleston, South Carolina, and seeing early iterations around 1913 at the Jungles Casino in New York's San Juan Hill.
Willie 'The Lion' Smith recalled a predecessor performed by Russell Brown under the name 'Geechie dance'.
on_screen: Map: United States · North America
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally a casual social and challenge dance among African-American communities, the Charleston became an emblem of post-WWI liberation, youth culture, and defiance of alcohol prohibition in American speakeasies.
In contemporary swing dance culture, it functions as both a high-energy solo showpiece and a core element within Lindy Hop social dancing and jam circles.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: Josephine Baker - rare topless dance clip & lost color Clara Bow film (https://archive.org/details/JosephineBaker-RareToplessDanceClipLostColorClaraBowFilm)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The Charleston can be danced solo, with a partner, or in group lines and circles.
Dancers maintain slightly bent knees with feet turned inward and outward, creating alternating knock-kneed and bow-legged positions while keeping feet at right angles to the leg at the ankle.
The arm action mirrors natural walking: as the left leg steps forward, the right arm moves forward while bent at the elbow and wrist.
Watch for Basic 8-Count Step, Savoy Kicks, Johnny's Drop.

Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Danced in place, traveling in stroll lines, or arranged in social circles and jam formats.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music for the 1920s Charleston features early hot jazz, ragtime, and stride piano played at rapid tempos ranging from 50 to 75 bars per minute (200 to over 300 beats per minute).
The fundamental rhythm incorporates the syncopated clave beat, which composer Gunther Schuller linked to the habanera and the Spanish Tinge.
Listen for the Piano, Trumpet, Trombone, Clarinet.
The pulse is 4/4.
Bright stride piano bass chords on downbeats matched with syncopated treble accents, driving brass melodies, and rapid banjo or drum backbeats.

Listen later: The Charleston — James P. Johnson; The Charleston — Golden Gate Orchestra

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: During the 1920s, women wore short flapper dresses or skirts adorned with hanging ribbons, fringe, sequins, or feathers designed to highlight dynamic leg and hip movements, paired with short 'à la garçonne' hair.
Men wore black pinstriped suits with bow ties or neckties.
Settings ranged from Broadway theaters and Parisian cabarets to American speakeasies, floor contests, and public stunts.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key historic figures include composer James P. Johnson, performer Elisabeth Welch, dancer Russell Brown, cabaret star Josephine Baker, film stars Bessie Love, Ann Pennington, Ginger Rogers, Joan Crawford, and dancers Santos Casani and Josie Lennard.

Variants include 1920s Solo Charleston, 20s Partner Charleston, 30s/40s Partner Charleston (incorporating jockey, side-by-side, and tandem positions), Collegiate Charleston, Crawl Charleston (a 1933 slow variation resembling a tango or waltz), and Black Bottom.
Rooted in African-American Juba and dockworker rhythms, the Charleston evolved through 1920s stage revues into social partner and solo forms.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Charleston Stroll is parent of Lindy Hop: Charleston steps were integrated directly into Lindy Hop during the 1930s and 1940s.
Charleston Stroll is sibling of Black Bottom: A contemporary 1920s trend featuring similar binary syncopated rhythms and hopping steps.
Charleston Stroll is child of Quickstep: Collegiate Charleston served as a direct precursor to the ballroom Quickstep.

scenes.title: Try one step
narration: Before we go, one step. Stand with knees slightly bent and feet turned slightly inward at ankles.
On counts 1-2, step or touch the left foot back without shifting full weight.
Count it: 1-2-3-4 then 5-6-7-8 (eight counts, two bars).
Chapter 1 takes it slowly from here.

scenes.title: Body and posture
narration: Upright torso with slight forward pitch; knees constantly flexed; ankles relaxed to allow inward/outward foot rotation.
Arms swing in counter-motion to legs, bent at 90 degrees at elbows and wrists; palms facing down or out.
Torso pulses rhythmic isolation; hips twist naturally with leg movement and foot rotation.

scenes.title: Step A — slowly
narration: Step 1: Stand with knees slightly bent and feet turned slightly inward at ankles.
Step 2: On counts 1-2, step or touch the left foot back without shifting full weight.
Footwork from the sources: Alternating weight transfers, toe touches forward and back, inward (knock-kneed) and outward (bow-legged) ankle twists.
Drill: Practice touch-step forward and back slowly without music.
on_screen: Instructor front view, then back view (student's perspective); repetitions per step: about 4
Counts on screen

scenes.title: Step B — the next layer
narration: Step 3: On counts 3-4, step onto the left foot, shifting full body weight onto it.
Step 4: On counts 5-6, touch the right foot forward while swinging left arm forward with bent elbow.
Drill: Add 90-degree elbow arm swings in opposition to leg movement.
on_screen: Instructor front and back view; slow, then half tempo

scenes.title: Put it together
narration: Step A, then Step B, without stopping. Slow first.
Now half tempo. Now full tempo.
Mirror: the instructor faces you and mirrors, so your right is your right.
on_screen: Split screen: front view / back view
Tempo label changes: slow → half → full

scenes.title: Common mistakes and what to avoid
narration: Avoid stiff knees or rigid ankles; avoid locking joints during rapid leg twists and high kicks.
on_screen: Side-by-side: source-supported correction

Options card: Seated or supported option: Perform the 8-count pattern seated in a sturdy chair, tapping toes back on counts 1-2, weight placing on 3-4, tapping forward on 5-6, and returning on 7-8 while swinging bent arms. · For children: Charleston Freeze Tag: Children dance the basic step in a circle and must freeze in a bow-legged or knock-kneed position when the music stops.
